summary: For ages 7–9, teach that a tropical rainforest is not one flat scene but a vertical stack of four layers — forest floor, understory, canopy, and emergent — each with different light, food, and space, and animals whose bodies are matched to their layer. Build the layers bottom-to-top, tie each adaptation to its layer's demands, and help children reason why so many species can live in one warm, wet, year-round habitat (the most species-rich land habitat on Earth, with the canopy the richest layer — a widely taught generalisation here drawn from unverified references). Core activities centre on matching animals to layers by their adaptations; supporting activities include a labelled cross-section to explore, a predict-reveal about which layer is busiest, a categorisation/matching check, and an optional field-biologist curiosity hook.
misconceptions: 'The rainforest floor is where most animals live' — the canopy holds the greatest abundance and diversity; the floor is dim and comparatively sparse.
'Rainforest and jungle are the same everywhere' — the structured layers create very different living conditions within one forest.
'Rainforests are hot deserts of trees' / it rains all the time — they are warm and consistently wet, but the defining traits are year-round warmth and high rainfall.
'Bright colours help animals hide' — many rainforest colours are warnings (poison) or signals, not camouflage.
'All rainforest animals live in trees' — each layer, including the floor, has its own specialised residents.

activities.title: Stock the rainforest: match animals to their layers
steps: Work with a vertical cross-section from the dark forest floor up to the sunlit emergent layer, with each layer labelled by its light level and food (fruit and leaves high up; litter and decomposers on the dim, damp floor).

Place animals into the layer where their body suits them: a howler monkey or prehensile-tailed creature and a sloth with hook-like claws into the canopy; a tapir, decomposers, and a ground-hunting jaguar on the forest floor; a camouflaged ambush animal such as a snake into the dim understory; a harpy eagle or large bat in the emergent layer. (Jaguars also climb into the understory, so the sim should accept that placement too.)
For each placement, say WHY the animal fits — name the adaptation (gripping tail, hooked claws, camouflage, strong flight) and the layer demand it meets.
Try a deliberate mismatch (e.g. put the gripping-tailed monkey on the floor, or the tapir up in the canopy) and describe what would go wrong.
activities.insight: An animal's body and its layer are a matched pair: adaptations such as a prehensile tail or hooked claws make an animal thrive in one layer and struggle in another. A rainforest packs in so much life precisely because its stacked layers create many different homes in one warm, wet place.

activities.title: Explore the four-layer cross-section
steps: Study a tall cross-section of the rainforest built bottom-to-top: forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent.

Reveal the signature animals in each layer and, for each, a 'why here?' note linking its body to the layer (prehensile tail gripping a branch, a sloth's hook-like claws, a tree frog's sticky toe pads).
Trace the light gradient from the bright emergent top to the dark floor and connect it to why canopy life differs from floor life.
Compare a 'species pile-up' of a rainforest against another habitat (including a local temperate wood) to see the sheer difference in number of kinds of animals.
activities.insight: One habitat contains many micro-environments stacked vertically; light and food change with height, and this structure is why the rainforest supports so many kinds of life.

activities.title: Predict then reveal: which layer is busiest?
steps: Look at a labelled rainforest cross-section or photo and predict which layer holds the most animals, saying why BEFORE any reveal.
Compare the prediction with the answer: scientists think the canopy, not the forest floor, is home to the most kinds of rainforest animals.

Discuss why the canopy is richest — bright light, fruit, and leaves up top — and why the floor is dim, with fewer plants growing and fewer kinds of animals, even though it is busy with decomposers and insects.
Answer follow-up prompts: 'What does a toucan find high up that it couldn't find on the floor?' and 'If all the tall canopy trees were cut down, what would happen to the toucan?'
activities.insight: Most children expect the floor to be busiest; surfacing and then revising that prediction makes the canopy's richness and its dependence on light and food memorable.

activities.title: Sort and match check
steps: Sort a set of rainforest animals into their correct layers.
Match adaptations to the layer demand they meet (gripping tail → canopy; camouflage and ambush → dim understory; foraging/decomposing → floor; strong flight → emergent).
Answer a short question on why rainforests hold so many species (warm, wet, year-round, many niches across stacked layers).
activities.insight: The child can categorise animals by layer and connect adaptations to layer demands, and can state why the habitat is so species-rich.

activities.title: Optional: canopy biologist curiosity hook
steps: Hear or read a short in-role account from a field biologist describing a canopy walkway and how scientists study the treetops.
Pose a question about how researchers reach and observe canopy animals that are hard to see from the ground.
activities.insight: Scientists study the rainforest in layers too; the hard-to-reach canopy requires special methods, which reinforces that it is a distinct, species-rich world.

checkQuestion: Here are two rainforest animals: a toucan and a jaguar. The toucan spends its days high up in the treetops; the jaguar lives down on the forest floor. Why don't they just live in the same place? What is different about the top of the rainforest and the bottom?
checkAnswer: The rainforest has layers with different conditions. The canopy at the top is bright and full of fruit, leaves and most of the animals, so a fruit-eating, tree-climbing bird like the toucan lives there. The forest floor is dark, damp and open, where a big ground hunter like the jaguar can prowl and stalk prey. Different layers offer different light, food and space, so different animals are suited to each.
